title: Re-evaluation of phosphoric acid–phosphates – di-, tri- and polyphosphates (E 338–341, E 343, E 450–452) as food additives and the safety of proposed extension of use
authors: EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Flavourings (FAF), Younes M, Aquilina G, Castle L, Engel KH, Fowler P, et al.
funder: European Food Safety Authority; requestor: European Commission; question numbers EFSA-Q-2011-00532 to -00543, EFSA-Q-2011-00618 to -00626, EFSA-Q-2011-00628 to -00630 and EFSA-Q-2018-00597; adopted 4 June 2019.
result: E 450 comprises disodium diphosphate (E 450(i)), trisodium diphosphate (E 450(ii)), tetrasodium diphosphate (E 450(iii)), tetrapotassium diphosphate (E 450(v)), dicalcium diphosphate (E 450(vi)), calcium dihydrogen diphosphate (E 450(vii)) and magnesium dihydrogen diphosphate (E 450(ix)); JECFA specifications carry the same INS sub-numbers. Formulae are Na2H2P2O7, Na3HP2O7, Na4P2O7, K4P2O7, Ca2P2O7, CaH2P2O7 and MgH2P2O7; synonyms include disodium pyrophosphate, tetrasodium pyrophosphate, tetrapotassium salt of diphosphoric acid, calcium pyrophosphate and acid calcium and acid magnesium pyrophosphate. Diphosphate, also named pyrophosphate, is M4P2O7; sodium diphosphates are made by neutralising phosphoric acid with sodium hydroxide and drying above 200 °C, which condenses phosphate groups. JECFA functional classes (Appendix A) include raising agent for E 450(i), (ii), (vi), (vii) and (ix), sequestrant for (i) and (iii), emulsifier for (ii), (iii), (v) and (vii), emulsion stabiliser for (ii), (vii) and (ix) and buffer, including acidity regulator, for (iii) and (vi). Phosphate additives are assumed to dissociate in the gastrointestinal tract; inorganic phosphorus from food additives is absorbed at about 80 to 90% as free orthophosphate, without metabolism, by passive diffusion and sodium-dependent active transport; NaPi-IIb (SLC34A2) predominates in the intestine and is modulated by active vitamin D and low phosphorus intake. About 200 mmol of phosphorus is filtered daily, 80% or more is reabsorbed in proximal tubules mainly via NaPi-IIa, and PTH and FGF-23 with Klotho influence reabsorption; excretion is via the kidney. In rats fed 5% tetrasodium diphosphate, diphosphate was undetected in faeces and urine, hydrolysis to orthophosphate in the gut was almost complete and about 85% was absorbed; toxicokinetic data on dicalcium and calcium dihydrogen diphosphate are lacking. The only significant adverse effect of phosphates in animal studies was kidney calcification and tubular nephropathy; a 90-day rat study of tetrasodium diphosphate gave a NOAEL of 500 mg/kg bw per day (116 mg P/kg bw per day). A group ADI of 40 mg/kg bw per day, expressed as phosphorus, was derived for E 338–341, E 343 and E 450–452 from a chronic rat NOAEL of 76 mg P/kg bw per day plus 91 mg P/kg bw per day background diet (167 mg P/kg bw per day) divided by an adjustment factor of 4; it covers phosphorus from all sources, natural ones included, and does not apply to people with moderate to severe reduction in renal function. Mean whole-diet exposure estimated from analytical data ranged across surveys from 16 mg P/kg bw per day in adults and the elderly to 85 mg P/kg bw per day in infants aged 12 weeks to 11 months; it exceeded the ADI at the mean for infants, toddlers and children, and at the 95th percentile also for adolescents (highest 95th percentile 123 mg P/kg bw per day, in toddlers). Exposure from food additives indicatively contributed 6 to 21% of total mean intake in all groups except infants and 12 to 30% in infants aged 12 weeks to 11 months. In the EU, phosphates (E 338–341, E 343, E 450–452) were authorised with maximum permitted levels of 500 to 20,000 mg/kg expressed as P2O5 in 104 uses and at quantum satis in four.
